alalal-e83039-d1e104.summary: Rubric of Article 17: whether faith has certainty prior to all knowledge.

alalal-e83039-d1e115.summary: Introduces the question on Augustine's words in Lombard's text: we believe in order to know.

alalal-e83039-d1e127.summary: First objection: Augustine in the Eighty-three Questions says some things are understood and believed at once.

alalal-e83039-d1e139.summary: Second objection: if all certainty is through knowledge, faith has no certainty before knowledge.

alalal-e83039-d1e150.summary: Third objection: all certainty of cognition comes from reason; faith is or involves cognition but lacks reason, so it has no certainty.

alalal-e83039-d1e166.summary: Sed contra: the foundation of any science is highly certain, so much more in divine science; faith is the foundation of divine science and life (1 Corinthians 3:11, with Ambrose's gloss that the foundation is faith in Jesus Christ), so it is most certain.

alalal-e83039-d1e200.summary: Solution: faith is in a certain way more certain than any art or demonstration. Certainty is twofold: of intellective truth, found in first principles, demonstrations from them, or what is accepted through them; and of affective truth, the truth according to piety (Titus 1:1), which is above reason and draws certainty not from rational principles but from a simple light like first truth that opens the eye to see first truth, as sunlight opens the eye. This light informs conscience and convinces by affect of the truth of what is believed and that one must tend toward it beyond reason's bounds. So a saint who knows mathematics would sooner deny that a triangle's angles equal two right angles than deny the truth of faith.
claims: Faith's certainty is affective, from a light like first truth, and exceeds the certainty of demonstration.
The believer would sooner deny a geometrical theorem than an article of faith.

alalal-e83039-d1e277.summary: This answers the last two objections.

alalal-e83039-d1e284.summary: Reply to the first: 'believing' is said in many ways; Augustine there uses it broadly for any consent to any truth, in which sense believing and understanding coincide in the sciences. Unless 'understanding' means grasping what the words signify, which precedes all consent, in the intellectual sciences and in the knowledge according to piety that faith is.

alalal-e83039.summary: Article 17 asks whether faith has certainty before all knowledge, as Augustine's 'we believe in order to know' implies. Objections hold that belief and understanding can coincide and that all certainty comes from knowledge or reason. Against them, faith is the foundation of divine science and so must be most certain. Albert distinguishes the certainty of intellective truth, grounded in principles and demonstrations, from the certainty of affective truth, the truth according to piety. The latter comes not from rational principles but from a simple light like first truth, which informs conscience and convinces by affect beyond reason's bounds. In this way faith is more certain than any demonstration: a saint would sooner deny a geometrical theorem than an article of faith. Augustine's simultaneous believing and understanding uses 'believe' broadly for any assent. Grasping what the words mean always precedes assent.
claims: Faith's certainty is affective, grounded in a light like first truth, and exceeds the certainty of demonstration.
Faith is the most certain foundation of divine science.
Grasping what the words mean precedes every assent, including the assent of faith.
